title: Employee Full Name And Initials
outcome: 🆕 new practice question — not attempted yet
watchOutFor: `||` returns NULL if any operand is NULL; `CONCAT()` treats NULL as an empty string.
problem: HR is printing name badges and needs each employee's display name, monogram initials and a lower-case login stem.
objective: For every employee, return the full name (`first_name last_name`), upper-case initials, and the last name in lower case.
expectedOutput:
| Column | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| employee_id | Employee identifier |
| full_name | First and last name separated by a space |
| initials | Upper-case first letters of first and last name |
| login_stem | Last name in lower case |

| employee_id | full_name | initials | login_stem |
|-------------|-----------|----------|------------|
| 1 | Nancy Davolio | ND | davolio |
| 2 | Andrew Fuller | AF | fuller |
| 3 | Janet Leverling | JL | leverling |
| 4 | Margaret Peacock | MP | peacock |

*(Sample rows are illustrative — the first few rows from the practice dataset, shown to convey shape/format; your data instance may differ.)*
approach:
1. Concatenate `first_name || ' ' || last_name` for the full name.
2. Take `LEFT(..., 1)` of each name, concatenate and wrap in `UPPER()`.
3. Apply `LOWER(last_name)` and order by `employee_id`.
mySolution:
SELECT
    employee_id,
    first_name || ' ' || last_name                    AS full_name,
    UPPER(LEFT(first_name, 1) || LEFT(last_name, 1))  AS initials,
    LOWER(last_name)                                  AS login_stem
FROM employees
ORDER BY employee_id;
solution:
SELECT
    employee_id,
    first_name || ' ' || last_name                    AS full_name,
    UPPER(LEFT(first_name, 1) || LEFT(last_name, 1))  AS initials,
    LOWER(last_name)                                  AS login_stem
FROM employees
ORDER BY employee_id;
referenceQuery:
SELECT
    employee_id,
    first_name || ' ' || last_name                    AS full_name,
    UPPER(LEFT(first_name, 1) || LEFT(last_name, 1))  AS initials,
    LOWER(last_name)                                  AS login_stem
FROM employees
ORDER BY employee_id;
why: `||` is the SQL-standard concatenation operator and is the most readable choice when the inputs are `NOT NULL` (both name columns are). `LEFT(text, n)` returns the first *n* characters, so two calls give the monogram. `UPPER`/`LOWER` only change letter case and leave other characters untouched, so they are safe for names with accents.
pitfalls: Using `||` on nullable columns: one NULL turns the whole result NULL — use `CONCAT()` or `COALESCE` there.
Using `+` for concatenation (SQL Server habit) — PostgreSQL raises an operator error.
Forgetting the space literal and producing `NancyDavolio`.
Calling `SUBSTRING(name, 0, 1)` — PostgreSQL positions start at 1, so this returns an empty string.

followups.question: What is the difference between `||` and `CONCAT()`?
followups.answer: `'a' || NULL` is NULL, while `CONCAT('a', NULL)` is `'a'`. `CONCAT_WS(' ', a, b)` also inserts a separator and skips NULL arguments.

followups.question: How would you capitalise only the first letter of each word?
How would you add the courtesy title when it exists?
followups.answer: `CONCAT_WS(' ', title_of_courtesy, first_name, last_name)` — the NULL title is skipped, so no leading space appears.

takeaway: `||` for NOT NULL inputs, `CONCAT`/`CONCAT_WS` when NULLs are possible; `LEFT`, `UPPER` and `LOWER` handle simple formatting.
